entry.title: Building DFIR Playbooks with Huddle
entry.content:
Most incident response playbooks I’ve seen live in one of two places: a wiki page nobody has opened since the tabletop, or someone’s head. When the alert fires at 2 a.m., neither one is much help. What responders actually need is short: what to do, in what order, who owns it, and what to do when the answer is “it depends.”

So I built Huddle, a browser-based tool for building DFIR playbooks out of reusable plays. You search a library of incident response actions, drag them into the phases of the IR lifecycle, wire them together with decisions, and hand responders a runbook they can actually work from. You can try it right now at jon.glass/huddle.

Goals

  • Built from plays, not prose. A play is one action with its steps, tools, artifacts, roles, timing and ATT&CK techniques. Playbooks are just plays arranged in order.
  • Organized by the lifecycle. Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery and Lessons Learned are the lanes everything sits in.
  • Something responders can use. A diagram is nice, but the output that matters is a checklist with owners and timestamps.
  • Extensible like CyberChef. Your own plays, your own libraries, and the whole playbook in a link.
  • Keep it local. Like Spoke, everything runs in the browser. There is no server and no account, and nothing gets uploaded.

Huddle ships with 69 plays across the six phases and five templates: Ransomware, Business Email Compromise, Compromised Credentials, Malware on Endpoint and Web Application Compromise. The templates are a fast start, but the best way to see how it works is to build one from scratch. Let’s do a credential-harvesting phishing playbook.

Step 1: Start with an Empty Playbook

Open Huddle. If you’ve used it before, pick New → Blank playbook. You get six empty lanes, one per phase, and a prompt offering the templates if you’d rather not start from zero.

A blank playbook. The library is on the left, the lifecycle lanes in the middle, and details on the right.

Click the name at the top and call it something useful. I went with Phishing: credential harvest.

Step 2: Add a Trigger and Your First Plays

Every playbook starts with what kicked it off. Drag Trigger from the row of buttons above the library into the Identification lane, and set its label in the right-hand panel to User reports a phishing email.

Now find plays. The search box matches titles, steps, tools, tags and ATT&CK IDs, so phishing, sign-in, Okta or T1078 all work. The library groups plays by phase and starts collapsed, so searching is usually faster than browsing. Drag a play onto the canvas and it snaps into the lane for its phase, or click the + on a card to drop it in without dragging.

Searching for “sign-in” and dragging Review identity provider sign-ins into Identification. The right-hand panel shows the play’s steps, tools and ATT&CK techniques.

For this playbook I added:

  • Identification: Triage the initial alert, Review identity provider sign-ins, Investigate mailbox activity
  • Containment: Reset credentials and revoke sessions, Remove malicious mail rules and purge phishing
  • Eradication: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA
  • Lessons Learned: Hold post-incident review, plus an End node

Step 3: Add a Decision and Connect Everything

Playbooks branch. Drag a Decision into Identification and ask the question that splits the response: Did the user enter credentials?

To connect two nodes, drag from the dot on the right side of one onto the other. Decisions have two dots: the green one is Yes and the red one is No.

Dragging from Investigate mailbox activity to the decision. The dashed line follows the mouse until you let go on a node.

Here, Yes goes to resetting credentials and revoking sessions, then on to purging the email. No skips straight to the purge. Both paths then run through MFA hardening, the post-incident review and the end.

Step 4: Tidy Up

Click Tidy and Huddle arranges everything into its lanes, following the arrows so the flow reads top to bottom and left to right. Click Fit (or press F) to see the whole thing.

The finished flow: 7 plays, 1 decision and 10 connections. The At a glance panel shows the mix of phases.

Step 5: Make It Yours

The library is generic on purpose. Your environment isn’t. Click any node and the This playbook section lets you change its title, set an owner and target time, rewrite the steps, and add notes for responders. These changes only apply to this playbook, so the library stays clean.

Reset credentials and revoke sessions, now owned by the Identity team with a 15-minute target and a note on exactly where to click.

If you want to reuse an edited play, Save as play turns it into one of your own. You can also create plays from scratch with + New play. Custom plays live in your browser under My plays, and they travel inside any playbook that uses them.

Step 6: Save, Share and Export

Press Ctrl+S (or click Not saved next to the name) and the playbook goes into My playbooks. From then on every edit saves automatically. My playbooks is where you open, rename, duplicate, export or delete them.

Share link copies a link with the entire playbook compressed into it, the same trick CyberChef uses. Anyone who opens it gets your playbook exactly as you left it, and since the data is after the #, it never gets sent to a server.

For responders who don’t live in Huddle, Export gives you:

  • Markdown runbook with numbered steps and checkboxes, ready for a wiki, a ticket or GitHub
  • Print / PDF runbook with a signature line for each step
  • Mermaid diagram that renders in GitHub, GitLab or Obsidian
  • CSV task list for a spreadsheet or ticketing import
  • Playbook JSON to keep in a repo
  • SVG of the diagram for slides and reports

The Markdown export. Plays come out in flow order, grouped by phase, with checkboxes for every step.

Step 7: Run It

When the alert actually fires, click Run. The playbook becomes a working checklist. Enter the incident ID, tick off steps as you go, and Huddle stamps each one with the time in UTC. At a decision you pick the branch, and the steps on the path you didn’t take are marked skipped. Every play has a notes box for findings, evidence IDs and who did what.

Run mode partway through. Progress is 2 of 8, the decision went Yes, and the No branch’s steps no longer count.

Export log downloads a Markdown incident log with every step’s status and a timestamped timeline, which is a great head start on the final report.

Extending Huddle

Like CyberChef, Huddle is configured through the URL:

  • ?lib=<url> loads an extra play library (JSON or CSV) and can be repeated
  • ?pb=<url> loads a playbook JSON from somewhere like your team’s repo
  • ?template=ransomware starts from a template
  • ?mode=run opens straight into run mode, and ?mode=view is read-only

A library is just a list of plays. Only title is required, and the phase accepts names like “Containment” or “Detection & Analysis”:

{
  "name": "Acme IR plays",
  "plays": [{
    "id": "ACME-001",
    "title": "Page the on-call IR lead",
    "phase": "Identification",
    "steps": ["Trigger the IR-Primary service", "Confirm acknowledgement within 15m"],
    "tools": ["PagerDuty"],
    "time": "15m"
  }]
}

A CSV with one play per row works too. An unknown phase becomes a new lane, so a “Comms & Legal” workstream running alongside the technical response is one column away. You can also Import a library file or load one From URL inside the app.

Plays for an AI-Assisted SOC

More SOCs are putting AI agents to work on triage and enrichment, and the playbooks need to say who does what. Steps that start with Agent: or Human: get labeled throughout Huddle. There’s an AI-Assisted SOC library built that way: 28 plays covering how you set the agent up, triage, approval-gated containment, and what to do when the agent itself gets manipulated by something like prompt injection. People approve anything that changes a system, declare incidents and own the final calls.

The AI-Assisted Alert Triage template. Each step is tagged AGENT or HUMAN, and the cards on the canvas show the split.

Load it with jon.glass/huddle/?lib=plays/ai-soc.json, then pick New → AI-Assisted Alert Triage.

Shortcuts

  • / jumps to search, and ↓ moves from the search box into the results
  • ↑ ↓ ← → move through the library or follow the flow on the canvas, and Enter adds the highlighted play
  • [ and ] switch between the library and the canvas
  • Ctrl+S saves to My playbooks
  • Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z undo and redo, Ctrl+D duplicates a node, and Del deletes it
  • F fits the diagram to the screen
  • ? opens the help, including every URL option

Try It

Open Huddle, pick New → Ransomware, and click Run. Thirty seconds later you’ll have a timestamped checklist and a good idea whether this is useful for your team.

The plays are general guidance, so adapt them to your environment before you lean on them in a real incident. If you build a library for your team or have plays you think belong in the core set, let me know.

entry.title: ADFIRWMC - 5.1 Did It Run? Evidence of Execution

link.title: ADFIRWMC - 5.1 Did It Run? Evidence of Execution

entry.content:
Welcome back. It has been a minute.

In Chapter 3 we built a list of files of forensic interest and added them to our collection script. In Chapter 4 we ran strings across everything to get our bearings. Now it is time for the structured part: actually parsing the artifacts and making them answer questions.

Chapter 5 is Windows disk artifact analysis, and it is big enough that I am breaking it into parts:

  • 5.1 Did It Run? Prefetch, Amcache, and ShimCache (you are here)
  • 5.2 Who Ran It? User registry hives and event logs
  • 5.3 What Did They Open, and From Where? Shortcuts and jump lists
  • 5.4 Where Did It Come From? USB and external devices
  • 5.5 Putting It All Together One timeline to rule them all

We are going to use the same scenario for every part.

The Scenario

Your antivirus console lights up Thursday morning. It quarantined EVILFILE.EXE from C:\Users\bob\AppData\Local\Temp\ on Bob’s workstation. The AV says it detected the file on Thursday, but the file’s timestamps say it landed on Tuesday. Your boss walks over and asks the only question anyone ever asks first:

“Did it run?”

“The file was there” is not an answer to that question. Lots of evil sits on disk and never executes. Lots of evil executes and then deletes itself. To answer the question you need artifacts that record execution, and you need to know exactly what each one does and does not prove.

Existed vs. Executed

Before we touch a single tool, burn this into your brain. Evidence falls into three buckets:

  1. The file existed. It was on disk at some point. ($MFT, USN Journal)
  2. Windows knew about it. The OS looked at it, inventoried it, or showed it in a folder. That does not mean it ran.
  3. The file executed. Something actually launched it.

Most of the arguments I have seen between analysts (and most of the bad reports I have read) come from treating bucket 2 like bucket 3. Each artifact below gets labeled with its bucket.

Tools Used

  • Eric Zimmerman’s Tools: PECmd, AmcacheParser, AppCompatCacheParser, Registry Explorer, and Timeline Explorer
  • PowerShell

Eric’s tools are free, they are maintained, and they are the de facto standard for this stuff. If you only take one thing from this chapter, take his tools.

Collection

Good news: if you followed along in Chapter 3, you already collected everything in this part. Prefetch, Amcache, and the SYSTEM hive are all in the collection script.

One fix. Registry hives on a live system are usually “dirty,” meaning recent changes are still sitting in the transaction logs (.LOG1 and .LOG2) and have not been written into the hive yet. The SYSTEM hive line from Chapter 3 already grabs everything in the config folder, but the Amcache line only grabs the hive itself. Swap it for this:

  • Line to add to collection script:
    • $filesigs += '^c:\\Windows\\AppCompat\\Programs\\Amcache\.hve(\.LOG[12])?$'

Keep the transaction logs in the same folder as the hive. Eric’s tools will notice them and replay them for you.

Prefetch

Bucket 3: Executed. This is your strongest evidence of execution on a workstation.

What It Is

Prefetch is a performance feature. When a program launches, Windows watches what files it loads in roughly the first ten seconds and writes that down, so the next launch can preload everything and start faster. The side effect is that Windows keeps a diary of what ran, when, and how often.

  • Location: C:\Windows\Prefetch\
  • File name: EXECUTABLENAME-HASH.pf, for example EVILFILE.EXE-1A2B3C4D.pf
  • The hash is calculated from the executable’s path. The same program run from two different folders gets two different .pf files. If you ever see two SVCHOST.EXE prefetch files and one hash you do not recognize, start asking questions.

What You Get

  • The executable name
  • Run count
  • Last run time, and on Windows 8 and later, the last eight run times
  • Volume information (serial number and creation time) for where it ran from
  • A list of the files and directories referenced during that first ten seconds

That last one is criminally underrated. It shows you the DLLs it loaded, the config files it read, and sometimes the files it dropped.

The .pf file’s own timestamps help too. The file is created a few seconds after the first run and modified a few seconds after the most recent run.

Gotchas

  • Prefetch is disabled by default on Windows Server. No .pf files on a server is normal, not suspicious.
  • It can be turned off on workstations too, through the EnablePrefetcher value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters. If a workstation has no prefetch, check that value.
  • There is a cap of 1,024 files on Windows 8 and later. The oldest entries roll off. On a busy machine, “no prefetch file” does not mean “never ran.”
  • Prefetch files are compressed on Windows 10 and later. The strings and grep tricks from Chapter 4 will not work on raw .pf files. Parse them first.

Parsing It

Point PECmd at the whole folder and get CSVs back:

PECmd.exe -d "C:\Cases\BOBPC\Prefetch" --csv "C:\Cases\BOBPC\Out"

Or one file with -f. Open the CSV in Timeline Explorer, or slice it with PowerShell. Here is my favorite trick: search every program’s loaded-file list for anything that touched a user’s Temp, Downloads, or AppData folders.

Import-Csv "C:\Cases\BOBPC\Out\*_PECmd_Output.csv" |
    Where-Object { $_.FilesLoaded -match '\\(TEMP|DOWNLOADS|APPDATA)\\' } |
    Select-Object ExecutableName, RunCount, LastRun |
    Sort-Object LastRun

That usually finds the bad thing and whatever helped it.

Back to Bob

PECmd shows EVILFILE.EXE with a run count of 3. The first run lines up with Tuesday afternoon, and the most recent run is Wednesday morning, a full day before the AV woke up. The files referenced include a DLL in Bob’s AppData\Roaming folder that nobody mentioned.

So yes, it ran. Three times. And now we have a second file to go find.

Amcache

Bucket 2: Windows knew about it. Not proof of execution by itself, but it gives you something Prefetch does not: a hash.

What It Is

Amcache is a registry hive that the Application Experience service uses to inventory programs on the system. It replaced RecentFileCache.bcf, which is a Windows 7 artifact. If you are not looking at Windows 7 machines anymore, you can drop that line from your collection script.

  • Location: C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve
  • It is a registry hive, so it opens in Registry Explorer just like any other.

What You Get

  • Full path of the file
  • SHA1 hash
  • File size, version info, publisher, and product name
  • The compile (link) time of the executable

The SHA1 is the prize. The AV quarantined EVILFILE.EXE and maybe even deleted it, but Amcache still has its hash. Look it up on VirusTotal and you might have your malware family before lunch.

Gotchas

  • An Amcache entry is not proof of execution. The inventory process records files that were installed, scanned, or simply present, not just files that ran. ANSSI research published in 2019 tested this thoroughly. Treat Amcache as “this file existed, and here is its hash,” then back it up with something from bucket 3.
  • The hash covers only roughly the first 30 MB of a file. For large files, the SHA1 in Amcache will not match the whole-file hash you calculate yourself. Malware is rarely that big, but installers are.
  • Key timestamps tell you when the entry was recorded, not when the program ran.

Parsing It

AmcacheParser.exe -f "C:\Cases\BOBPC\Amcache.hve" --csv "C:\Cases\BOBPC\Out"

You get several CSVs back. The file entries are the ones you want for this question. Filter on the path or the file name.

Back to Bob

Amcache has an entry for EVILFILE.EXE in Bob’s Temp folder, with a SHA1. It also has an entry for that DLL from Prefetch. Two hashes, two VirusTotal searches.

ShimCache (AppCompatCache)

Bucket 2: Windows knew about it. This one has burned more analysts than any other artifact I know of, so read the gotchas twice.

What It Is

The Application Compatibility Cache tracks executables Windows evaluated to decide whether they need a compatibility fix (a “shim”). It lives in the SYSTEM hive:

  • HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache, value AppCompatCache

What You Get

  • Full path of the executable
  • The file’s last modified time
  • The order of entries, most recent first

Gotchas

  • The timestamp is the file’s last modified time, not the execution time. Say that out loud. This is the single most common ShimCache mistake, and it shows up in real reports.
  • On Windows 10 and later, there is no reliable execution flag. An entry means Windows saw the file. Simply browsing a folder in Explorer can add entries.
  • ShimCache is written to the registry at shutdown or reboot. Until then, the newest entries live in memory. If Bob’s machine has not rebooted since Tuesday, the SYSTEM hive you collected may not contain EVILFILE.EXE at all.

Why Bother, Then?

  • It keeps paths of files that are long gone, including ones that never ran.
  • The order tells you roughly what Windows saw before and after something else.
  • The stored modified time is a great timestomping check. If ShimCache says a file was modified in 2024 and the $MFT says 2009, someone has been messing with timestamps.

Parsing It

AppCompatCacheParser.exe -f "C:\Cases\BOBPC\SYSTEM" --csv "C:\Cases\BOBPC\Out"

Bonus: BAM

Bucket 3: Executed, with a user attached.

On Windows 10 (version 1709) and later, the Background Activity Moderator keeps a last-execution time for programs, per user. It lives in the SYSTEM hive:

  • HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\bam\State\UserSettings\<User SID>

Each value is a program path and its last execution time. Its memory is short, and its behavior has shifted between Windows builds, so treat it as a nice bonus when it is there rather than something you count on. Open the SYSTEM hive in Registry Explorer and browse to the key.

The interesting part is the SID. BAM does not just say the program ran; it says whose session ran it. That is the question for 5.2.

Why Do You Care?

Here is the cheat sheet for this part:

Artifact Bucket Timestamp means Hash? Biggest gotcha
Prefetch Executed First run, last 8 runs No Off on servers; 1,024-file cap
Amcache Windows knew When it was inventoried SHA1 Entry is not execution
ShimCache Windows knew File’s last modified time No Not execution time; written at shutdown
BAM Executed Last run, per user No Short memory

No single artifact answers “did it run?” by itself. Prefetch is the closest thing to a yes, Amcache gives you the hash, ShimCache backs up the path and catches timestomping, and BAM points at a user. Together they make an answer you can defend.

Back to Bob, One More Time

So far we know:

  • EVILFILE.EXE ran three times, starting Tuesday afternoon (Prefetch)
  • It loaded a DLL from Bob’s AppData\Roaming folder (Prefetch)
  • We have SHA1 hashes for both files (Amcache)
  • BAM ties the last run to Bob’s SID

Which leads to the next question. Was it actually Bob, or just Bob’s account? That is a job for 5.2: Who Ran It?

Happy hunting.

entry.title: Reverse-Engineering a FitRx EMS App into a Python Controller

link.title: Reverse-Engineering a FitRx EMS App into a Python Controller

entry.content:
Short on time? Explore this post as a graph in Spoke: the decompiled app, the protocol, the Python controller, its safety features and what’s next, all as clickable nodes.

Why I went down this road

I recently tore my ACL, and part of getting my quad working again is retraining it with a TENS machine.

I ended up with a working Python script that drives a FitRx wireless EMS unit from my MacBook, and I got there by decompiling the vendor’s Android app. I did most of the digging alongside Gemini, pasting terminal output back and forth until the protocol fell out.

The unit I used: the FitRx Electrode Wireless Massager from Walmart.

The goal was simple. I had a cheap stimulator, and I wanted custom routines it doesn’t offer: a slow ramp up, a hold, a ramp down, a rest, repeated for a set time. Eventually I want Claude to be able to kick off and adjust those sessions for me.

The catch: the FitRx companion app wouldn’t even install on my Android phone. It was flagged as too old for my “too new” phone. So if I wanted app control at all, I had to build it myself.

Decompiling the APK

My first attempt at sharing the app’s code was a mistake: I pasted the raw APK contents, which is just a ZIP archive full of compressed class files. Useless. The right tool is jadx, which turns the APK back into readable Java:

brew install jadx
jadx -d fitrx_src /path/to/FitRx.apk
cd fitrx_src

Then I started grepping for the obvious Bluetooth write call:

grep -rn "writeCharacteristic" .

Every hit was inside sources/com/inuker/bluetooth/library/. That’s Inuker BluetoothKit, an Android BLE wrapper library. It hides the raw GATT calls, so the app’s own code never calls writeCharacteristic directly. I needed to find where the app called into the library instead.

Grepping the app’s own package for “write” only turned up Android Parcel boilerplate. So I listed the package to get the lay of the land:

ls -R sources/com/fitrx/songhua/massagetool/

Two folders stood out: BlueteethTool/ (yes, “Blueteeth”) and massagemain/, which holds the main control screen.

Following the trail

Device names. BlueteethTool/b.java is the connection manager. Its scan callback only accepts devices with these names, which told me what to look for when scanning:

if (hVar.b().equals("HRK-016B")
    || hVar.b().toLowerCase().startsWith("FitRx Wireles".toLowerCase())
    || hVar.b().toLowerCase().startsWith("FitRx 7772".toLowerCase())) {

HRK-016B looks like the OEM board model. The same file also counts connections in SharedPreferences and has a check that returns false after 35 or 130 connects. I never confirmed where that check is used, so I’m filing it under “interesting” rather than “explains everything.”

The Bluetooth client. BlueteethTool/c.java is just a singleton that hands out the Inuker client. So I grepped for every caller:

grep -rn "c\.a()" sources/com/fitrx/songhua/massagetool/

The interesting hits were in MassageMainActivity.java. One method, c0, is the single choke point where every command leaves the app. It takes a hex string, converts it to bytes, and writes it:

private void c0(String str) {
    Log.e("BLE", "postMessage : " + str);
    com.inuker.bluetooth.library.a aVarA = c.a();
    com.fitrx.songhua.massagetool.f.b bVar = this.D;
    aVarA.c(bVar.f934b, bVar.c().c, this.D.c().f936b,
            com.inuker.bluetooth.library.n.c.c(str), this.H);
}

The UUIDs. bVar.c() and bVar.b() come from f/b.java, which walks the device’s GATT services and picks characteristics by prefix. There are two profiles, chosen by whether the device name starts with “FitRx 7772”:

if (d()) {  // "FitRx 7772"
    if (svc.startsWith("0000fff0") && chr.startsWith("0000fff5")) this.e = cVar;  // write
    if (svc.startsWith("0000fff0") & chr.startsWith("0000fff4")) this.f = cVar;   // notify
} else {
    if (svc.startsWith("0000ae3a") && chr.startsWith("0000ae3b")) this.e = cVar;  // write
    if (svc.startsWith("0000ae3a") && chr.startsWith("0000ae3c")) this.f = cVar;  // notify
}

The commands. Finally, the methods just above c0 build the strings. Here’s intensity:

public void W(int i2) {
    String str = String.format("%02d", Integer.valueOf(i2));
    c0("ACAD06A0000000" + str + "BCBD");
}

Mode and timer follow the same pattern with A1 and A2. Each one also has a twin that sends something completely different for the 7772 profile.

Decoding the protocol

The standard profile uses a fixed 10-byte frame. It opens with AC AD 06, then a command byte, three parameter bytes, the value, and closes with BC BD. No checksum.

The 7772 strings looked like noise until I decoded the hex as ASCII. 41542B434D4F44453D302C is just AT+CMODE=0,. That profile speaks plain-text AT commands ending in \r\n.

Command Standard (HRK-016B) 7772 variant
Intensity ACAD06A0000000{level:02d}BCBD AT+CSTR=1,{level}\r\n
Mode ACAD06A1000000{mode:02d}BCBD AT+CMODE=0,{mode}\r\n
Timer (minutes) ACAD06A2010100{minutes:02X}BCBD AT+CDCLK=00{mm}00\r\n
Timer off ACAD06A200000000BCBD AT+CDCLK=000000\n\r\n
Write / notify UUIDs ae3b / ae3c on service ae3a fff5 / fff4 on service fff0

Two quirks are worth noting. Intensity and mode are formatted as decimal digits (%02d), but the timer is formatted as hex (Integer.toHexString). So a 20-minute timer is sent as 14. And the 7772 “timer off” string really does have that odd \n\r\n ending; I copied it from the app as-is.

In Python, sending a frame is a one-liner with bleak:

WRITE_UUID = "0000ae3b-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"
await client.write_gatt_char(WRITE_UUID, bytes.fromhex("ACAD06A000000003BCBD"), response=False)  # level 3

Building the Python controller

macOS supports BLE natively, and bleak uses CoreBluetooth under the hood, so no dongle is needed. Two Mac-specific notes: your terminal needs Bluetooth permission under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Bluetooth, and macOS shows devices by a UUID instead of a MAC address.

Scan and connect. I reuse the app’s own name filter, then subscribe to the notify characteristic:

devices = await BleakScanner.discover(timeout=7.0)
for d in devices:
    name = (d.name or "").strip()
    if any(name.startswith(p) for p in ["HRK-016B", "FitRx Wireles", "FitRx 7772"]):
        self.device = d
        break

self.client = BleakClient(self.device.address)
await self.client.connect()
await self.client.start_notify(self.notify_uuid, self._notification_handler)

Commands. Each device command is a thin wrapper that clamps its input and builds the frame from the table above:

async def set_intensity(self, level: int):
    level = max(0, min(level, 9))
    await self._send_payload(f"ACAD06A0000000{level:02d}BCBD")

async def set_timer(self, minutes: int):
    if minutes == 0:
        await self._send_payload("ACAD06A200000000BCBD")
    else:
        await self._send_payload(f"ACAD06A2010100{minutes:02X}BCBD")

Ramps and duty cycles. The unit only knows eight fixed modes and ten intensity levels. Everything else, like ramping and work/rest cycles, I do in software by stepping the intensity over time:

async def _ramp(self, start_lvl, end_lvl, duration_sec):
    steps = abs(end_lvl - start_lvl)
    if steps == 0 or duration_sec <= 0:
        await self.massager.set_intensity(end_lvl)
        return
    interval = duration_sec / steps
    direction = 1 if end_lvl > start_lvl else -1
    current = start_lvl
    for _ in range(steps):
        current += direction
        await self.massager.set_intensity(current)
        await asyncio.sleep(interval)

The session loop then runs ramp up, hold, ramp down, and rest until the session time runs out.

The CLI. Gemini’s first version had --pps and --phase-duration flags for frequency and pulse width. They didn’t do anything; they were only printed. The unit doesn’t expose those settings over Bluetooth, so I removed them. The flags that are left all do something real:

python3 fitrx_orchestrator.py \
  --mode 1 \
  --target-intensity 4 \
  --duty-cycle 10 20 \
  --ramp 5 \
  --ramp-down 2 \
  --timer 20

Safety, and what the AI got wrong

This is a script that controls current going into my body, so I designed it to fail toward “off.”

  • Hardware timer first. Before anything else, the script sets the unit’s own timer to the session length. If my Mac sleeps, crashes, or loses Bluetooth, the unit should still shut itself off.
  • Ctrl+C always sends a stop. A signal handler turns Ctrl+C into a task cancellation, so the finally block always runs and sends level 0.
  • Loud failure. If the software stop itself fails, the script says so plainly instead of exiting quietly.
  • Raw telemetry only. I log notification bytes with timestamps but don’t interpret them, because I haven’t confirmed the format yet.
async def main(cfg):
    task = asyncio.current_task()
    asyncio.get_running_loop().add_signal_handler(signal.SIGINT, task.cancel)
    await SessionOrchestrator(cfg).run()

# ...inside run():
finally:
    try:
        await self.massager.stop()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"!! SOFTWARE STOP FAILED ({e}).")
        print("!! Turn the unit off with its power button or remove the pads.")

The real emergency stop is still the power button or pulling a pad. The software stop depends on Bluetooth working.

AI was genuinely useful for the grind: knowing jadx, recognizing Inuker BluetoothKit, and telling me which file to cat next. But it also stated guesses as facts. It gave me names and frequencies for all eight modes, current ranges per intensity level, and a battery and pad-fault format for the notifications. None of that came from the code. It also called my final script “production-grade” without catching that the hardware timer backstop had never been tested. Treat its confident details as hypotheses.

What’s next

  • Test the hardware timer backstop with no pads attached: start a session, kill the script, confirm the unit shuts off on time
  • Confirm that level 0 means no output, and that timer 0 doesn’t mean “run forever”
  • Log notification bytes next to each command I send and start decoding them
  • Look up the real mode names in the app’s resources
  • Wrap the controller as a tool so Claude can start and adjust sessions

Appendix: the full script

Here’s the complete fitrx_orchestrator.py. The 7772 profile is untested; I only have the standard HRK-016B hardware.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
FitRx / HRK-016B session controller (BLE, macOS).

Runs ramp / hold / ramp-down / rest cycles using the unit's own mode presets
(1-8) and intensity levels (0-9), with the hardware timer set as a backstop.
Logs raw notification bytes from the device for study; it does not interpret
them, because the device's status format hasn't been confirmed yet.

The real emergency stop is the unit's power button or removing a pad.
The software stop below depends on Bluetooth working.
"""

import argparse
import asyncio
import signal
import sys
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

from bleak import BleakClient, BleakScanner

# GATT UUIDs from the decompiled app
UUID_MAP = {
    "standard": {
        "service": "0000ae3a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb",
        "write": "0000ae3b-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb",
        "notify": "0000ae3c-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb",
    },
    # Untested: no hardware with this profile has been tried.
    "7772": {
        "service": "0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb",
        "write": "0000fff5-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb",
        "notify": "0000fff4-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb",
    },
}

TIMER_MIN, TIMER_MAX = 5, 40  # the unit's advertised timer range, in minutes


@dataclass
class SessionConfig:
    mode_preset: int = 1
    target_intensity: int = 4
    ramp_up_seconds: float = 5.0
    ramp_down_seconds: float = 2.0
    work_seconds: float = 10.0
    rest_seconds: float = 20.0
    total_minutes: int = 20


class FitRxMassager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.client = None
        self.device = None
        self.variant = "standard"
        self.write_uuid = None
        self.notify_uuid = None
        self._t0 = time.monotonic()

    def _notification_handler(self, sender, data: bytearray):
        """Log raw notification bytes with a timestamp. No interpretation."""
        t = time.monotonic() - self._t0
        print(f"[RX {t:8.2f}s] {data.hex(' ').upper()}")

    async def scan_and_connect(self):
        print("Searching for FitRx / HRK-016B...")
        devices = await BleakScanner.discover(timeout=7.0)

        for d in devices:
            name = (d.name or "").strip()
            if any(name.startswith(p) for p in ["HRK-016B", "FitRx Wireles", "FitRx 7772"]):
                self.device = d
                break

        if not self.device:
            raise RuntimeError("FitRx device not found. Make sure the unit is on and blinking.")

        print(f"Found {self.device.name} [{self.device.address}]")
        self.variant = "7772" if "7772" in self.device.name else "standard"
        if self.variant == "7772":
            print("Warning: the 7772 profile is untested.")
        self.write_uuid = UUID_MAP[self.variant]["write"]
        self.notify_uuid = UUID_MAP[self.variant]["notify"]

        self.client = BleakClient(self.device.address)
        await self.client.connect()
        print(f"Connected ({self.variant} profile).")

        await self.client.start_notify(self.notify_uuid, self._notification_handler)
        print("Logging notifications.")

    async def _send_payload(self, hex_string: str):
        if not self.client or not self.client.is_connected:
            raise ConnectionError("BLE client is not connected.")
        await self.client.write_gatt_char(self.write_uuid, bytes.fromhex(hex_string), response=False)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.08)

    async def set_mode(self, mode: int):
        mode = max(1, min(mode, 8))
        print(f"[TX] mode {mode}")
        if self.variant == "standard":
            await self._send_payload(f"ACAD06A1000000{mode:02d}BCBD")
        else:
            await self._send_payload(f"AT+CMODE=0,{mode:02d}\r\n".encode().hex())

    async def set_intensity(self, level: int):
        level = max(0, min(level, 9))
        print(f"[TX] level {level}")
        if self.variant == "standard":
            await self._send_payload(f"ACAD06A0000000{level:02d}BCBD")
        else:
            await self._send_payload(f"41542b435354523d312C{f'{level:X}'.encode().hex()}0D0A")

    async def set_timer(self, minutes: int):
        print(f"[TX] timer {minutes} min" if minutes else "[TX] timer off")
        if self.variant == "standard":
            if minutes == 0:
                await self._send_payload("ACAD06A200000000BCBD")
            else:
                await self._send_payload(f"ACAD06A2010100{minutes:02X}BCBD")
        else:
            if minutes == 0:
                await self._send_payload("41542B4344434C4B3D3030303030300A0D0A")
            else:
                await self._send_payload(f"41542B4344434C4B3D3030{f'{minutes:02d}'.encode().hex()}30300D0A")

    async def stop(self):
        print("[Software stop] Setting level 0 and clearing timer...")
        await self.set_intensity(0)
        await self.set_timer(0)

    async def disconnect(self):
        if self.client and self.client.is_connected:
            try:
                await self.client.stop_notify(self.notify_uuid)
            except Exception:
                pass
            await self.client.disconnect()
            print("Disconnected.")


class SessionOrchestrator:
    def __init__(self, config: SessionConfig):
        self.cfg = config
        self.massager = FitRxMassager()

    async def _ramp(self, start_lvl: int, end_lvl: int, duration_sec: float):
        steps = abs(end_lvl - start_lvl)
        if steps == 0 or duration_sec <= 0:
            await self.massager.set_intensity(end_lvl)
            return
        interval = duration_sec / steps
        direction = 1 if end_lvl > start_lvl else -1
        current = start_lvl
        for _ in range(steps):
            current += direction
            await self.massager.set_intensity(current)
            await asyncio.sleep(interval)

    async def run(self):
        c = self.cfg
        try:
            await self.massager.scan_and_connect()

            # Hardware timer first, so the unit shuts itself off even if this script dies.
            await self.massager.set_timer(c.total_minutes)
            await self.massager.set_mode(c.mode_preset)
            await self.massager.set_intensity(0)

            print("\nSession:")
            print(f"  Duration     : {c.total_minutes} min (hardware timer set)")
            print(f"  Mode preset  : {c.mode_preset}")
            print(f"  Peak level   : {c.target_intensity} of 9")
            print(f"  Work / rest  : {c.work_seconds}s / {c.rest_seconds}s")
            print(f"  Ramp up/down : {c.ramp_up_seconds}s / {c.ramp_down_seconds}s")
            print("  Ctrl+C to stop. Power button or removing a pad is the real emergency stop.\n")

            total_seconds = c.total_minutes * 60
            elapsed = 0.0
            cycle = 1
            while elapsed < total_seconds:
                print(f"[Cycle {cycle}] Ramp up 0 -> {c.target_intensity} over {c.ramp_up_seconds}s")
                await self._ramp(0, c.target_intensity, c.ramp_up_seconds)
                elapsed += c.ramp_up_seconds

                print(f"[Cycle {cycle}] Hold level {c.target_intensity} for {c.work_seconds}s")
                await asyncio.sleep(c.work_seconds)
                elapsed += c.work_seconds

                print(f"[Cycle {cycle}] Ramp down {c.target_intensity} -> 0 over {c.ramp_down_seconds}s")
                await self._ramp(c.target_intensity, 0, c.ramp_down_seconds)
                elapsed += c.ramp_down_seconds

                if elapsed >= total_seconds:
                    break

                print(f"[Cycle {cycle}] Rest at level 0 for {c.rest_seconds}s\n")
                await asyncio.sleep(c.rest_seconds)
                elapsed += c.rest_seconds
                cycle += 1

            print("\nSession complete.")
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            print("\nInterrupted.")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"\nError: {e}")
        finally:
            try:
                await self.massager.stop()
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"\n!! SOFTWARE STOP FAILED ({e}).")
                print("!! Turn the unit off with its power button or remove the pads.")
            try:
                await self.massager.disconnect()
            except Exception:
                pass


def parse_args() -> SessionConfig:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="FitRx BLE session runner with ramps and duty cycles")
    p.add_argument("--mode", type=int, default=1, choices=range(1, 9),
                   help="Hardware mode preset 1-8 (default: 1)")
    p.add_argument("--target-intensity", type=int, default=4, choices=range(1, 10),
                   help="Peak level 1-9 (default: 4)")
    p.add_argument("--duty-cycle", nargs=2, type=float, metavar=("WORK", "REST"), default=[10.0, 20.0],
                   help="Hold and rest times in seconds (default: 10 20)")
    p.add_argument("--ramp", type=float, default=5.0, help="Ramp-up seconds (default: 5)")
    p.add_argument("--ramp-down", type=float, default=2.0, help="Ramp-down seconds (default: 2)")
    p.add_argument("--timer", type=int, default=20, choices=range(TIMER_MIN, TIMER_MAX + 1),
                   metavar=f"{TIMER_MIN}-{TIMER_MAX}",
                   help=f"Session length in minutes, {TIMER_MIN}-{TIMER_MAX} (default: 20)")
    a = p.parse_args()

    work, rest = a.duty_cycle
    if work <= 0 or rest < 0 or a.ramp < 0 or a.ramp_down < 0:
        p.error("work time must be positive; rest and ramp times can't be negative")

    return SessionConfig(
        mode_preset=a.mode,
        target_intensity=a.target_intensity,
        ramp_up_seconds=a.ramp,
        ramp_down_seconds=a.ramp_down,
        work_seconds=work,
        rest_seconds=rest,
        total_minutes=a.timer,
    )


async def main(cfg: SessionConfig):
    # Turn Ctrl+C into a task cancellation so the stop in `finally` always gets
    # sent, on every Python version, instead of the loop being torn down first.
    task = asyncio.current_task()
    asyncio.get_running_loop().add_signal_handler(signal.SIGINT, task.cancel)
    await SessionOrchestrator(cfg).run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cfg = parse_args()
    try:
        asyncio.run(main(cfg))
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("\nAborted. If the unit is still running, use its power button.")
        sys.exit(1)

entry.title: Spoke: Seeing the Relationships in Your CSVs

link.title: Spoke: Seeing the Relationships in Your CSVs

entry.content:
A lot of security data is really a graph pretending to be a spreadsheet. A process tree is parent and child PIDs. An insider risk case is users, hosts, files and USB devices tied together by actions. You can grep through those rows all day, but the story usually pops the moment you can see the shape of it.

So I built Spoke, a browser-based tool that turns rows like who → did what → to what into an interactive graph. You can try it right now at jon.glass/spoke.

The Insider risk sample with jsmith selected. The Details panel lists every action in time order.

Goals

  • Low code. Anyone on the team should be able to use it by visiting a web page. No installs, no database.
  • Versatile. The same tool should handle process parent-child chains and insider risk webs without changing code.
  • Keep the data local. Insider risk data is sensitive. Nothing should be uploaded anywhere.

That last one drove the whole design. Everything runs in the browser. Node.js is only used to build it, and the output is a single static page, which is how Spoke lives right here on this GitHub Pages blog. Your files never leave your machine because there is no server to send them to. There is also a Download button that gives you the whole app as one HTML file for offline or air-gapped use.

Under the hood it is Cytoscape.js for the graph, dagre for hierarchical layouts, PapaParse and SheetJS for reading files, and Vite to bundle it.

The Workflow

The sidebar walks you through five steps: Load, Map, Filter, View and Export. If you just want to poke at it, the Samples menu has four datasets ready to go:

  • Insider risk: a user’s activity before leaving, with files, USB and email
  • Process tree: a small malware process hierarchy
  • Endpoint activity: a noisy three-sheet Excel export for practicing filtering
  • EDR export: repeated process names and IDs, to show why combined keys matter

1. Load

Spoke takes CSV or Excel (.xlsx, .xlsm, .xlsb, .xls, .ods). For workbooks with several sheets you can pick one, or choose All matching sheets to stack every sheet with the same columns. A sheet column records where each row came from, and summary or README tabs are skipped.

2. Map

Every row becomes an edge between two nodes. You pick the Source, Target, Relationship, optional Source type and Target type (which drive the colors and legend), and a Time column. Spoke guesses all of these from your column names, so a lot of the time you just check them and hit Build graph.

The feature I care most about here is combined keys. In real EDR data, a name alone isn’t unique. There are dozens of cmd.exe processes, and process IDs get reused across machines. If you map on the name alone, every cmd.exe collapses into one node and the tree turns into nonsense.

+ Combine with another column lets you build a node’s identity from several columns, so ProcessName + ProcessId + Hostname becomes cmd.exe (3400, WS-01). A preview shows what the IDs will look like, and Spoke suggests name/ID pairs automatically, adding the host column when it sees more than one machine. If your data has a ProcessGuid, mapping on that alone is the most reliable option.

Process name, ID and host combined into one key, so each process instance is its own node.

3. Filter

Big exports are mostly noise, so the filter takes a regular expression and applies it as you type. You can match against node names, the relationship label, or any column in the row, such as severity, user or command line. Then either Hide the matches, or Show only the matches plus context: one to three hops of neighbors, or the entire connected group. Actual matches are outlined in purple.

A few examples against the Endpoint activity sample:

Pattern Settings Result
svchost\|chrome\|teams\|onedrive\|msmpeng Node names, Hide 224 nodes drop to a few dozen and the attack chain on WS-07 stands out
high\|critical Any column, Show only Just the serious events
rundll32 Node names, Show only, +1 hop One process and everything it touched

Hiding routine processes takes the Endpoint activity sample from 224 nodes to 28, leaving the attack chain on WS-07.

The built-in help includes a regex cheat sheet, since not everyone who touches this will live in regex the way we do.

The Time Bar

When there is a time column, a histogram appears under the graph showing when events happened, so bursts stand out. Drag across it to pick a window, click a bar to zoom into that slice, or type exact times. Nodes stay put as you scrub, so you can watch activity come and go.

Fade instead of hide keeps out-of-window items as faint ghosts for context, and Keep undated holds onto rows with no timestamp, like an org chart link. You can switch the whole app between UTC and local time. It reads ISO 8601, common date formats, Unix epoch seconds or milliseconds, and Excel dates. The time window and the regex filter stack: something is shown only if it passes both.

On the Insider risk sample, clicking the tall bar on the evening of 18 Oct narrows the graph to just the late-night downloads and USB copies.

One click on the histogram narrows the Insider risk sample to the late-night hour on 18 Oct.

4. View

Two layouts cover most cases:

  • Process Tree for hierarchies like parent → child processes
  • Relationship Web, a force-directed layout for “who touched what” questions

Clicking a node highlights its full chain, everything upstream and downstream, and fades the rest. Click rundll32.exe in a process tree and you immediately see how it got there. Search outlines matches in orange without hiding anything, and you can adjust label size and font, or set edge labels to show only on hover to keep dense graphs readable.

Selecting rundll32.exe highlights the full chain from explorer.exe through Outlook, Word, cmd and PowerShell.

The Details panel is where a lot of the investigation actually happens. For a node, it shows its type, its number of connections, and an Activity list of every relationship in time order, with severity, IPs, command lines and any other columns. Severity, risk or priority columns are color-coded. Click a name to jump to that node. For an edge, you get the full original row from your file.

5. Export

  • PNG or JPG at 1×, 2× or 4× (good for print), or SVG so it stays sharp in slides and reports
  • CSV of the original rows behind what’s visible, which loads straight back into Spoke and is handy for passing along a trimmed dataset
  • JSON of visible nodes and edges with their full records and the filter used

Exports match the screen, so anything filtered out or outside the time window is left out.

Plays Nicely with CyberChef

Send to CyberChef opens the visible rows in CyberChef in a new tab, ready for decoding, extracting or reformatting. It uses CyberChef’s trick of putting the data after the # in the link, which browsers never send to a server, so it stays local there too.

Share Links

Copy share link packs the loaded file, compressed, together with your column mapping, layout, filter and time window. Whoever opens the link sees exactly the same view.

The important caveat: the data is in the link. Anyone with the link can see it, and links end up in browser history. Treat a share link like the file itself. Browsers also cap links at about 2 MB, so for big datasets share a filtered CSV export instead.

Linking from Other Tools

Because the data rides in the URL, scripts and other tools can open Spoke pre-loaded. Put base64 of a CSV or Excel file after #input=, gzip-compressed or not, and optionally set the mapping and view ahead of it:

https://jon.glass/spoke/#src=parent&tgt=child&layout=tree&input=cGFyZW50LGNoaWxk...

Supported settings include:

  • src, tgt: source and target columns, or a JSON list to combine them, e.g. ["ProcessName","ProcessId"]
  • rel, stype, ttype, time: the other column mappings
  • layout: tree or web
  • re, scope, mode, depth, case: the filter
  • from, to, undated, fade: the time window

Values need to be URL-encoded, and anything left out is guessed as if you had opened the file normally. That makes it easy to have a triage script or SIEM query spit out a link that drops an analyst straight into the right view.

Shortcuts

  • ? opens the help
  • / jumps to the filter box
  • [ hides or shows the sidebar
  • F fits the graph to the screen
  • Esc clears the selection

Try It

Open Spoke, pick Samples → Insider risk, and click the jsmith node. The whole chain lights up and the Details panel lists everything jsmith did, in order.

If you work in DFIR or insider risk and have an export format you’d like it to handle better, let me know.

link.title: What ChatGPT Wrote When I Asked It to Blog

entry.content:
This is what I got from ChatGPT when I provided the following prompt:

Write a 500 word technical blog post about the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API to perform Incident Response with Python examples

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is a comprehensive, cloud-based endpoint security solution that provides real-time protection against a wide range of cyber threats. It offers an API that allows security teams to integrate the platform with their existing security tools and workflows. In this blog post, we will explore how to use the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API to perform incident response with Python examples.

Before we dive into the technical details, it’s important to note that using the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API requires a valid subscription to the service. If you do not have access to the platform, you can sign up for a free trial to test the API.

The Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API provides a rich set of features for incident response. These include:

  • Retrieving alerts and incidents
  • Getting details about devices and endpoints
  • Querying security events and alerts
  • Retrieving and analyzing files
  • Managing remediation actions To use the API, you will need to authenticate with Azure Active Directory (AAD) and obtain an access token. This token will be used to make requests to the API endpoints. Here is an example of how to obtain an access token using the AAD Authentication Library (ADAL) in Python:
tenant_id = 'your_tenant_id'
client_id = 'your_client_id'
client_secret = 'your_client_secret'

context = adal.AuthenticationContext(f'https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant_id}')
token = context.acquire_token_with_client_credentials('https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com', client_id, client_secret)
access_token = token.get('accessToken')

Once you have obtained an access token, you can use it to authenticate your requests to the API endpoints. Here is an example of how to retrieve a list of all alerts:

import requests

url = 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/alerts'
headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {access_token}'}
response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
alerts = response.json()

This will retrieve a JSON object containing information about all alerts in the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint platform.

To retrieve information about a specific alert, you can use the alert ID to make a request to the API. Here is an example:

alert_id = 'your_alert_id'
url = f'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/alerts/{alert_id}'
response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
alert = response.json()

This will retrieve a JSON object containing detailed information about the specified alert.

You can also use the API to retrieve information about a specific device or endpoint. Here is an example:

device_id = 'your_device_id'
url = f'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/machines/{device_id}'
response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
device = response.json()

This will retrieve a JSON object containing information about the specified device or endpoint.

Another useful feature of the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API is the ability to retrieve and analyze files. Here is an example of how to retrieve a file and analyze it using the API:

file_id = 'your_file_id'
url = f'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/files/{file_id}'
response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
file_content = response.content

analysis_url = 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/analysis'
data = {'content': file_content}
response = requests.post(analysis_url, headers=headers, data=data)
analysis_result = response.json()

This will retrieve the contents of the specified file and submit it to the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint cloud for analysis. The API will return a JSON object containing the analysis result.

Finally, you can use the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint API to manage remediation actions.

entry.title: Running Arbitrary Commands with Live Response

link.title: Running Arbitrary Commands with Live Response

entry.content:
Running Arbitrary Commands on an Endpoint via the API

Microsoft Defender’s Live Response is a delightful addition to your Incident Response toolbelt, but it does have a particularly irksome deficiency. As of publication, it does not allow execution of arbitrary commands. I know. Ridiculous, right? Well, there is a simple fix for this…

C:\windows\system32\cmd.exe /c $args

yeah…that simple.

All we need to do now is upload it to our Live Response Library like we did in my previous post…

Uploading cmd.ps1 to the Live Response Library

script = """
         C:\windows\system32\cmd.exe /c $args
         """
fileobj = StringIO(script)

  • Maybe your command takes longer than 10 minutes to run.
  • Maybe your output is too large for the buffer Live Response is using to pull back STDOUT.

I am sure there are other reasons to send to a file instead of just reading the STDOUT manually.

Limitations of the Machine Action API

  1. Rate limitations for this API are 10 calls per minute (additional requests are responded with HTTP 429).
  2. 25 concurrently running sessions (requests exceeding the throttling limit will receive a “429 - Too many requests” response).
  3. If the machine is not available, the session will be queued for up to 3 days.
  4. RunScript commands time out after 10 minutes.
  5. Live response commands cannot be queued up and can only be executed one at a time.
  6. If the machine that you are trying to run this API call is in an RBAC device group that does not have an automated remediation level assigned to it, you’ll need to at least enable the minimum Remediation Level for a given Device Group.
  7. Multiple live response commands can be run on a single API call. However, when a live response command fails all the subsequent actions will not be executed.
  8. Parameters are a pain in the ass to encode across PowerShell and Batch; it is probably best to stick with PowerShell

entry.content:
I have decided to dust off the ol’ blog to start documenting some of my more recent endeavors leveraging the Microsoft 365 Security suite to perform Incident Response. Since I prefer to talk to APIs more than people, this seemed like a good opportunity to explore the different components of the ecosystem through the language of Python. Generic instructions are being provided to get you started but there are a lot of nuances with the environment and I can’t bring myself to document them all.

Getting Started

  1. Go here and get yourself a free 3 month license for Defender for Endpoint
  2. Click next and agree until it stops asking. Literally have no clue what I agreed to.
  3. Go to Microsoft 365 Defender.
  4. Go to Settings > Endpoints > Onboarding, grab an onboarding script, and onboard a device to your environment. Reference
  5. Reboot the device. You shouldn’t have to but it makes everything go faster.
  6. Head to Azure and build yourself an App.
  7. Go to YOUR APP > Certificates & secrets and make yourself a New client secret. Copy that down because you can only look at that once. We will need that later.
  8. Go to YOUR APP > API Permissions and Click Add a Permission.
  9. When the Request API permissions side screen pops up, click on APIs my organization uses. Type “WindowsDefenderATP” in the search box.
  10. Click on Application permissions Select EVERYTHING. Go nuts. Hit Update Permissions
  11. Now before you click away, Click Grant admin consent to YOUR DOMAIN. This should turn all orange “Not granted for”s into green “Granted for”s.
  12. Go to the YOUR APP > Overview page and gather your Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID. We will need the Tenant ID, App ID, and Client Secret to play with the API.
  13. Go to YOUR APP > Authentication page and under Platform configurations:
    • Click Add Platform
    • Click Web
    • Add https://portal.azure.com as a Redirect URI
  14. Navigate over to Conditional Access > Classic policies and disable that [Windows Defender ATP] Device policy or…you know, join your computer to this Domain. Your call.

Those are the rough strokes. Is it more complicated than that? Yes. I encourage everyone to RTFMs from Microsoft on spinning up a new M365.

Getting an Auth Token

To talk to the API, we will be leveraging the msal module to query Graph while changing the scope to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint’s API. This is the product of a lot of trial and error BUT the benefit of this is to multifactor the API so we can leverage the API via Jupyter Notebooks without having secret keys lying around everywhere.

import msal
import json
import requests
from datetime import datetime
from msal_extensions import *
import urllib3
urllib3.disable_warnings()

tenantID = '11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111'
clientID = '22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222'
authority = 'https://login.microsoftonline.com/' + tenantID
scope = ["https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/AdvancedQuery.Read"]
username = 'JonathanGlass@HalfFullofSecurity.onmicrosoft.com'
result = None
tokenExpiry = None

def msal_delegated_device_flow(clientID, scope, authority):
    print("Initiate Device Code Flow to get an AAD Access Token.")
    print("Open a browser window and paste in the URL below and then enter the Code. CTRL+C to cancel.")

    app = msal.PublicClientApplication(client_id=clientID, authority=authority)
    flow = app.initiate_device_flow(scopes=scope)

    if "user_code" not in flow:
        raise ValueError("Fail to create device flow. Err: %s" % json.dumps(flow, indent=4))

    print(flow["message"])
    result = app.acquire_token_by_device_flow(flow)
    return result

# Get a new Access Token using the Device Code Flow
